steps: Run workshops with your stakeholders to agree the KPIs and the business questions each team needs Adobe Analytics to answer.
Map each requirement to a dimension or metric and to the Analytics variable that will collect it, in a shared requirements sheet.
Write the solution design document, the blueprint of your analytics implementation, and review it with your stakeholders for sign-off.
Hand the document to your team with a simple process for keeping it current as your site and your questions change.
asks: Stakeholders from each team for the KPI and business-question workshops
An owner on your team who keeps the solution design document current
risk: A design that tries to track everything: we tie every variable to an agreed business question, so the implementation stays focused and easy to maintain.
outcome: You have a signed-off solution design document that ties each business question to the dimension, metric and Analytics variable that answers it.

steps: Create the development and production report suites, and enable and name the conversion variables, success events and props from the solution design.
Add the processing rules and bot rules your data needs, testing each one in the development report suite before production.
List all your channels with your marketing team, then configure marketing channels so every visitor hit is categorized to the right channel.
Set up classification sets for your campaign tracking codes, with a naming convention for new codes agreed with your campaign team.
deliverables: Configured variables, success events and props
asks: Your marketing team's full list of channels and how each one is identified
Your campaign tracking code formats, and an owner for the naming convention
risk: Hits falling into the wrong channel: we list every channel with your marketing team first and test the rules on development data before production.
outcome: Your report suites collect the variables in your solution design, with your bot rules in place and every visitor hit categorized to the right marketing channel.

steps: Specify the data layer with your developers, page type by page type and event by event, from the variables in the solution design.
Set up the datastream, the tags property and the Web SDK extension, the recommended path for new Web SDK implementations.
Map data elements to the Analytics variables, so each value in the data layer reaches the variable the solution design names.
Validate every page type and event in development against a test plan, then publish to production and recheck the top reports.
deliverables: Datastream, tags property and Web SDK extension
asks: Developers who can build the data layer into your site templates
Admin access to create the datastream and the tags property
An agreed release window for publishing to production
risk: Data that breaks when pages change: we write the data layer specification with your developers and validate every page type before publishing.
outcome: Your site sends the data your solution design calls for to Adobe Analytics through the Web SDK extension, validated before it went live.

steps: Agree the priority questions with each team, and sketch the Analysis Workspace project and visualizations that will answer each one.
Build the segments, calculated metrics and alerts behind each project, named and described so your team can find and reuse them.
Build the agreed Analysis Workspace projects, review them with each team, and share and schedule them with the people who need them.
Save company templates from the finished projects, so your team starts new analyses from agreed segments and metrics.
asks: The priority questions for each team, in ranked order
A reviewer from each team to test the projects against their questions
risk: Projects nobody opens: we build each one from a question a team has agreed, and review it with that team before it is shared.
outcome: Your teams answer their priority questions in shared Analysis Workspace projects, built on agreed segments, calculated metrics and alerts.

steps: Map your teams to the report suites, tools and components each one needs, and agree the access model with your admins.
Set up product profiles in the Admin Console from that access model, and assign your users to them.
Assign identity and sensitivity labels to the report suite's variables with your privacy team, and record each label and the reason for it.
Train your analysts and business users on Analysis Workspace, with exercises on your own data and a short guide for each group.
deliverables: Product profiles in the Admin Console
Identity and sensitivity labels on variables
asks: An Admin Console administrator who can create product profiles and assign users
A privacy contact who agrees the label for each variable
The names and roles of the people to train
risk: Too much access, or too little: we agree the access model by team first, then test each product profile with a real user before rollout.
outcome: Each team reaches only the report suites and tools it needs, variables carry their privacy labels, and your users build their own analyses in Analysis Workspace.

steps: Inventory your current Adobe Analytics tags extension setup, and choose with your team the rules and data elements to bring into the Web SDK upgrade assistant.
Map your Analytics variables to XDM, and review each Web SDK action the upgrade assistant adds to your rules.
Test the new library in development, and compare its reports with your current reports for an agreed period before publishing.
Publish to production in an agreed window, with a rollback plan to the current library if the comparison breaks after launch.
asks: Access to your current tags setup and its development environment
An agreed release window for publishing the new library
An analyst who signs off the report comparison
risk: Reports that shift after the move: we compare the new library against your current reports before publishing, and keep a rollback plan ready.
outcome: Your Adobe Analytics data collection runs on the Adobe Experience Platform Web SDK, with reports compared against your current ones before go-live.

steps: Agree with your data team the columns, report suite and delivery frequency, hourly or daily, for each data feed and export.
Set up the cloud account and location, and create the data feed with the agreed columns.
Schedule the Data Warehouse requests your data team needs, and check the first deliveries arrive complete and load into your platform.
asks: Access to your cloud storage, and a data team contact who owns it
The columns and reports your data team needs, and how often
risk: Feeds that arrive but cannot be used: we agree the columns with your data team and test that the first delivery loads into your platform.
outcome: Your data team receives raw Adobe Analytics data in your own cloud storage, and the scheduled Data Warehouse requests it needs, for use in your other platforms.

steps: Analyze your priority journeys and campaigns each month in Analysis Workspace, and look for changes worth acting on.
Run a Focused Review after each site release: check that the metrics and dimensions behind your top KPIs still collect correctly.
Fix or log any collection issue found, with the release it came from and an owner for each one.
Report findings and next steps to your team each month, and agree the journeys and campaigns to analyze next.
deliverables: Monthly findings and next steps report
Focused Review results after each release
asks: Notice of each site release, with what it changed, before it goes live
An owner on your team who agrees next month's priorities
risk: A release that quietly breaks tracking: we run a Focused Review after each one, so gaps behind your top KPIs are caught early.
outcome: Each month you have findings and next steps on your priority journeys, and a check that your top KPIs still collect correctly.

steps: Agree the identity type and single sign-on setup with your IT team, and set them up in the Admin Console.
Create product profiles by team in the Admin Console, with the services each team gets.
Set automatic assignment rules, add your users in bulk, and test sign-in with a pilot group before inviting everyone.
deliverables: Identity type and single sign-on setup
Users added, with pilot sign-in results
asks: An IT contact who manages your identity provider and single sign-on
Your user list by team, with the services each team needs
risk: Users locked out at launch: we test single sign-on with a pilot group before the rest of your users are added.
outcome: Your teams sign in to Acrobat with single sign-on and receive the right licenses and services automatically, by team.

steps: List the platforms your teams run, and agree with your IT team the features and preferences each package should set.
Build the Acrobat packages in the Admin Console for each platform you run.
Configure the features and preferences with the Acrobat Customization Wizard, and test each package on a pilot group of machines.
Agree with your IT team how updates are run, and hand over the tested packages for organization-wide deployment.
asks: An IT contact who runs software deployment on your machines
A pilot group of users on each platform you run
risk: A setting that disrupts work across the whole organization: we test each package on a pilot group before organization-wide deployment.
outcome: Your IT team deploys tested Acrobat packages, with features and preferences set for your organization and an agreed way to run updates.

steps: Decide with your team which groups get the generative AI features, and where your policy requires them turned off.
Assign the licenses and product profile services to the agreed groups, on the Named User licenses that AI Assistant requires.
Turn the features off where your policy requires, and test the setup with a pilot user from each group.
Train each group on summaries, questions with citations and shared PDF Spaces, using documents from their own work.
asks: Your policy on generative AI use, and who decides exceptions
The groups to include, and a pilot user from each one
risk: AI features reaching a team your policy excludes: we agree the groups first and test each product profile before training begins.
outcome: The agreed teams use AI Assistant for summaries, questions with citations and shared PDF Spaces, within the limits your policy sets.

steps: Map the document steps your application needs, with sample files, expected volumes and where each file is read from and written to.
Set up server-side credentials and connect your application to the PDF Services API in a development environment.
Build the agreed operations, such as creating PDFs from Office files or HTML, text recognition, combining, compressing, protecting and exporting.
Test each operation on your sample files, including error handling and retries, then deploy with a runbook for your team.
deliverables: Test results on your sample files
asks: Developers and access to the application that will call the API
Sample documents for each workflow, and where they are stored
risk: Files that fail in production: we test every operation on your own sample documents, the difficult ones included, before go-live.
outcome: Your application runs its document steps through the PDF Services API automatically, with files read from and written to your own storage.

steps: Agree the documents to generate with your team, such as contracts, invoices or letters, and collect the approved wording for each.
Build each template in Microsoft Word with template tags for text, tables, images and conditions.
Define the JSON data each template merges, and map it to the fields that hold it in your system.
Connect the Document Generation API to your system, and review generated samples with your document owners before sign-off.
deliverables: JSON data definition for each template
asks: The current documents and approved wording for each template
A document owner who signs off each template
Developers with access to the system that supplies the data
risk: A generated document with wrong or missing content: we test each template against sample data that covers every condition before sign-off.
outcome: Your system produces contracts, invoices or letters from approved Word templates, filled with your own data and without manual editing.

steps: Agree the pages that show PDFs, the embed mode for each one, and which tools visitors see.
Set up a client ID for each domain, and add the PDF Embed API to your pages or app.
Pass the viewer events to your analytics, and test the viewer on each agreed page and browser before release.
deliverables: Embedded PDF viewer on the agreed pages
Test results by page and browser
asks: The domains and pages where PDFs will be shown
A web developer, or access to your site's code
Your analytics contact for the viewer events
risk: A viewer that works on one domain and fails on another: we set up and test a client ID for every domain before release.
outcome: Visitors read PDFs inside your pages with the tools you chose, and your analytics records how they use them.

steps: Agree the document sets, native and scanned, and the search, data or AI system each one feeds, with sample files.
Build the pipeline that sends your PDFs to the PDF Extract API and collects the text, tables and figures, as structured JSON or Markdown.
Map the output, reading order and page layout included, to the fields your target system expects, and load it.
Check extraction quality on a sample from each document set, agree with your team the fixes for files that fall short, and hand over a runbook.
deliverables: Output mapping to your target systems
Quality check results by document set
asks: Sample PDFs from each document set, native and scanned
Access to the search, data or AI system that receives the content
risk: Content that loses its structure on the way: we check a sample from each document set, tables included, before the full run.
outcome: Text, tables and figures from your PDFs arrive in your search, data or AI systems as structured content, in reading order.

steps: Inventory your backlog of untagged PDFs, and rank the documents by how often people use them and how complex they are.
Run the backlog through the Accessibility Auto-Tag API in batches, and read the tagging report for each document.
Correct in Acrobat what tagging alone does not settle, such as alt text, complex tables, titles and reading order.
Check a sample of finished documents with assistive technology, and record each document's status in the inventory.
deliverables: Ranked inventory of the PDF backlog
asks: Access to the PDFs in your backlog and where they are published
Your accessibility lead, to agree priorities and review samples
risk: Auto-tagged output is not guaranteed to comply fully with WCAG and PDF/UA, so we review and correct each document after tagging.
outcome: Your backlog of PDFs carries the structure tags assistive technology needs, with the remaining issues corrected in Acrobat.

steps: Agree the document types to seal, such as invoices and statements, and the seal's appearance for each one.
Connect the PDF Electronic Seal API to your organization's certificate, hosted by your trust service provider under the Cloud Signature Consortium standard.
Apply the seal in your document flow, and test sealed samples of each document type with your compliance team before go-live.
deliverables: Seal appearance for each document type
Sealed sample documents and test results
asks: Your trust service provider contact and the certificate credentials for sealing
A compliance reviewer who approves the sealed samples
risk: A seal that fails or shows the wrong details: we test sealed samples of every document type with your compliance team before go-live.
outcome: Your invoices, statements and other official PDFs carry your organization's electronic seal, to demonstrate their integrity and authenticity.

steps: Agree the document flows with your team: what triggers each one, the files involved and where the results are saved.
Set up the Adobe PDF Services connector in your Microsoft Power Automate environment with its credentials.
Build the flows that convert, combine, protect or generate documents on files in OneDrive, SharePoint or another storage connector.
Test each flow on sample files, and hand over a guide your team uses to change and monitor the flows.
deliverables: Document flows in Microsoft Power Automate
asks: A Power Automate administrator who can add the connector and its credentials
Sample files, and the folders each flow uses
risk: Flows that stop when a folder or file changes: we test each flow on real sample files and name an owner on your team to watch for failures.
outcome: Your teams' document tasks run as Microsoft Power Automate flows on files in OneDrive, SharePoint or other storage, without manual steps.

steps: Map your teams to the Acrobat tasks that matter to them, such as editing, combining, protecting, redacting and requesting signatures.
Train each team on its own tasks, with exercises on documents like the ones they use every day.
Train your administrators on licenses, packages and updates, and hand over a guide for users and one for administrators.
deliverables: Training sessions for users and administrators
asks: The names and roles of the people to train
Time from each team for the sessions
risk: Training that does not stick: we teach each team only the tasks it does, on documents like its own, and leave a guide behind.
outcome: Your teams handle their everyday Acrobat tasks themselves, and your administrators run licenses, packages and updates on their own.

steps: Review Document Transaction usage against your allowance each month, and flag any trend that will need action.
Investigate and fix failed jobs, and record the cause of each one so it does not repeat.
Update templates and flows as your documents change, testing each change before it goes live.
asks: Notice of changes to your documents, with the new wording
An owner on your team for the monthly review
risk: Running past your Document Transaction allowance: we track usage each month and flag the trend early, so you can plan ahead.
outcome: Your document automation keeps running each month, with usage tracked, failed jobs fixed and templates in step with your documents.

steps: Map your business units to Acrobat Sign groups, each with its own settings, branding and templates, and agree the structure with your team.
Create the groups, name the account and group administrators, and add users with the report access each one needs.
Set up sign-in through the Adobe Admin Console with single sign-on, and test it with a pilot group before rollout.
deliverables: Single sign-on through the Adobe Admin Console
asks: Your business units, and who administers each one
An IT contact who manages your single sign-on
Your user list, by business unit
risk: A structure that does not match how teams work: we agree the groups with each business unit before any settings or templates are built.
outcome: Each business unit works in its own Acrobat Sign group with its own settings, and your users sign in with single sign-on.

steps: Review your policies with your legal, security and brand teams, and record the setting each policy calls for.
Configure your company name, logo and email branding, the signature preferences and the send settings, for the account and each group.
Set the security settings, and connect the external archive that receives a copy of every signed agreement.
Test a full agreement in each group, from sending to the archived copy, and record the settings for your administrators.
deliverables: Settings record by account and group
asks: Your signature, security and records policies
Your logo and brand guidance for agreement emails
The archive location that receives signed agreements
risk: A setting that breaks a policy: we record each setting against the policy that calls for it and test a full agreement before rollout.
outcome: Your Acrobat Sign account carries your brand, follows your security policies and archives a copy of every signed agreement.

steps: Rank your agreements by how often they are sent, and agree with your team which ones become library templates.
Build each template with signature, date and data fields for each signer, in the authoring environment or with text tags.
Set who may use and edit each template, and test each one with a sample signing before release.
Record each template's fields and owner in a template inventory, so document revisions stay under control.
deliverables: Library templates for your most used agreements
asks: Your most used agreements, in their current approved versions
An owner for each template who approves its fields
risk: A field placed for the wrong signer: we run a sample signing of every template before it is released to senders.
outcome: Your senders start each common agreement from a reusable library template, with the right fields set for every signer.

steps: Map each regular agreement type with your team: who signs, in what order, which documents go out and who gets copies.
Build the workflow templates in the Custom Workflow Designer, with recipients and routing, documents and fields, email copies, expiration and passwords.
Write instructions for senders on each workflow, and test every workflow end to end before release.
deliverables: Workflow templates in the Custom Workflow Designer
asks: The routing and approval rules for each regular agreement type
A sender from each team to test the workflows
risk: Agreements routed to the wrong person: we map each routing with your team and test every workflow end to end before release.
outcome: Your senders send each regular agreement type from a workflow that sets the recipients, routing and documents for them.

steps: Agree with your team which agreements people start themselves, and the participants and counter-signers for each one.
Create each signable web form with its participants, counter-signers and the signer authentication your policy requires.
Embed the web forms on your website or share them as links, and test each one from signing to counter-signature.
deliverables: Web forms embedded or shared as links
asks: The pages where each web form will appear, and a web contact who can add it
The counter-signer for each web form
risk: A form that collects signatures with too little proof of identity: we agree the signer authentication for each form with your team first.
outcome: People start and sign your agreements themselves on your website or from a link, and your counter-signers complete them.

steps: List with your team the agreements you send to many people and the merge fields each one fills, then set up a Send in Bulk parent template for each.
Set up the CSV file with recipients and merge fields, and test a small send to your own team first.
Show your team how to track the agreements a bulk send creates, and follow up on each person's progress.
deliverables: Parent template for each bulk agreement
asks: The agreements you send to many people, and the data each one merges
An owner who prepares the CSV recipient list
risk: Sending the wrong data to many people at once: we test each bulk send on a small internal list before the real one.
outcome: Your team sends one agreement to many people at once, each with their own document, and tracks each person's progress.

steps: Rank your agreement types by risk with your legal and compliance teams, and agree the identity check each one needs.
Set up the chosen checks, such as Acrobat Sign authentication, a phone or knowledge-based check, or a provider on the Digital Identity Gateway.
Set the default identity check for each group, and enable digital signatures where the law or your policy asks for them.
Test each check with a sample agreement, and record which agreement types use which check.
deliverables: Identity check for each agreement type
asks: Your legal and compliance view on which agreements need stronger identity checks
Your digital identity provider contact, where one is used
risk: Checks so strict that signers give up, or so light they fail an audit: we match each check to the risk of the agreement.
outcome: Each kind of agreement asks its signers for the identity check it needs, with digital signatures where the law or your policy requires them.

steps: Agree the retention period for each kind of agreement with your records and legal teams, from your records policy.
Agree where signed copies and audit reports are kept before Acrobat Sign deletes them, and test that they arrive there.
Set the data governance rules that delete agreements and their data after each retention period, and record them for your auditors.
deliverables: Record of where signed copies and audit reports are kept
asks: Your records policy and the retention period for each kind of agreement
A records or legal contact who signs off the rules
risk: Agreements deleted before a copy is kept: we make sure signed copies and audit reports reach your own store before any rule is turned on.
outcome: Agreements and their data are deleted on your records schedule, with signed copies and audit reports kept where your policy says.

steps: Map the agreement flow with your developers: what your system sends, from which templates, and what must come back once it is signed.
Set up the API application and OAuth for the Acrobat Sign REST API, and build the calls that send agreements from templates with your system's data.
Build the endpoint that receives the HTTPS POST for each subscribed webhook event, and return signed documents and field data to your system.
Test the full flow with your developers, including errors and agreements that are never signed, before go-live.
deliverables: Webhook endpoint that returns signed documents and data
asks: Developers and access to the system that will send agreements
A URL your system can receive webhook events on
risk: A missed event that leaves a record without its signed document: we test every event path, errors included, before go-live.
outcome: Your system sends agreements from templates with its own data, and signed documents and field data return to it automatically.

steps: Agree with your Salesforce admin which records send which agreements, and the record fields each agreement uses.
Install the Acrobat Sign for Salesforce package from the AppExchange in a sandbox, and set up the permission sets.
Build the agreement templates with their data mappings and merge fields, and add buttons that send for signature from a record.
Test each agreement from the record to signature, then move the setup to your production org.
deliverables: Installed Acrobat Sign for Salesforce package
Agreement templates with data mappings and merge fields
Send for signature buttons on records
asks: A Salesforce admin with rights to install packages in your org
The records and agreements to include, with sample data
risk: Wrong data merged into an agreement: we test each template's data mappings on sample records before it reaches your production org.
outcome: Your Salesforce users send agreements for signature from a record, filled with that record's data.

steps: Agree with your Microsoft 365 admin which users get the add-ins, and deploy them from the Microsoft admin center to a pilot group first.
Connect the add-ins for Teams, Outlook, Word and PowerPoint to your Acrobat Sign account, and test sending from each one.
Show your teams how to send and track agreements from the apps they work in, with a short guide for each app.
deliverables: Acrobat Sign add-ins deployed to agreed users
Connection to your Acrobat Sign account
asks: A Microsoft 365 admin who can deploy add-ins from the admin center
The users or groups that get the add-ins
risk: Add-ins that appear for some users and not others: we deploy to a pilot group first, then widen to everyone agreed.
outcome: Your teams send and track agreements from Teams, Outlook, Word and PowerPoint, without switching to another app.

steps: Agree with your HR systems team the Workday business processes that need signatures, and the documents each one sends.
Set up the OAuth relationship between Acrobat Sign and your Workday tenant, and the service account for the Workday group.
Add the business process steps that send documents for signature, starting in a test tenant.
Test each process from start to signed document with your HR team, then move it to production.
deliverables: Business process steps that send for signature
asks: A Workday administrator with rights to change business processes
The business processes and documents to include
risk: A business process that stalls at the signature step: we test each one end to end with your HR team before it goes live.
outcome: Your Workday business processes send documents for signature as one of their steps, with no separate tool for your HR team.

steps: Group your users by role into senders, template authors and administrators, and plan the sessions for each group.
Train senders on sending, tracking and reminders, and template authors on fields, templates and workflows, using your own agreements.
Train administrators on users, groups, settings and reports, and hand over a guide for each role.
deliverables: Sessions for senders, template authors and administrators
asks: The names and roles of the people to train
Time from each group for the sessions
risk: Senders falling back to old habits: we train each role on its own agreements, so the first real sends happen during training.
outcome: Your senders, template authors and administrators each run their part of Acrobat Sign themselves, with a guide to refer to.

steps: Run agreement reports each month on completion rates and time to sign, and review which templates and workflows stall.
Update the templates and settings behind the stalls, and agree each change with its owner before it goes live.
Add, move and remove users and groups as your teams change, and report the month's changes to your team.
asks: Notice of joiners, leavers and team changes each month
An owner who approves changes to each template
risk: Agreements that stall without anyone noticing: we review completion rates and time to sign every month and fix the templates behind the delays.
outcome: Each month you see how your agreements perform, and your templates, settings, users and groups stay current.

steps: Agree with your team the user groups the DAM needs, from administrators to contributors and readers, and who belongs in each.
Add your users to the Adobe Admin Console organization, create the user groups and attach the AEM Assets product profiles to them.
Agree with your team the Cloud Manager program and environments for the DAM, and record them in a setup record.
Test sign-in and access with a user from each group before the rest of your users are invited.
deliverables: Users, groups and AEM Assets product profiles
Cloud Manager program and environment record
asks: An Admin Console administrator for your organization
Your user list, with the group each person belongs to
Access to your Cloud Manager program and its environments
risk: People reaching assets they should not, or missing ones they need: we agree the groups first and test each one before inviting everyone.
outcome: Your users reach AEM Assets through agreed groups and product profiles, on the Cloud Manager program and environments set for the DAM.

steps: Run workshops with your asset users on how they search, by brand, product, campaign or channel, and review your current library.
Design the folder hierarchy under /content/dam, with naming rules, and agree it with your team before any assets are loaded.
Build the controlled tag taxonomy under /content/cq:tags, and agree how it sits beside the smart tags AEM applies automatically.
Create the custom metadata forms with your business-specific fields, and test search on sample assets with your users.
asks: Asset users from each team for the search workshops
A taxonomy owner who approves tags and metadata fields
risk: A structure that suits one team and not the rest: we design from how every team searches, and test it on sample assets first.
outcome: Your assets sit in an agreed folder hierarchy with controlled tags and custom metadata, so people find them and reuse them in every channel.

steps: Inventory your library with your team, decide what moves and what retires, and stage it in Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Dropbox or OneDrive.
Map your existing metadata to the agreed fields, and prepare the CSV files that load it for each asset.
Run a pilot Bulk Import and metadata load on a sample, check assets, metadata and smart tags, then import the full library in agreed batches.
Load the metadata from the CSV files, and reconcile asset counts and sample metadata against your inventory before sign-off.
asks: Access to your current library and the cloud storage it will be staged in
A library owner who decides what moves and signs off the result
risk: Assets that arrive without their metadata: we run a pilot import on a sample and reconcile counts and metadata before signing off.
outcome: Your library is in AEM Assets with its metadata, reconciled against the inventory and ready to search.

steps: List with your team the renditions and metadata each channel needs, such as the sizes and formats for web, social and print.
Configure the processing profiles on the upload folders for those renditions, metadata and image processing.
Add any post-processing workflows, then upload test assets to each folder and check every rendition before your teams start uploading.
deliverables: Rendition and metadata needs by channel
Processing profiles on the upload folders
asks: Your channel owners' rendition needs, such as sizes and formats
Sample assets to test each upload folder
risk: Renditions that do not fit a channel: we agree each channel's needs first and test every profile with real assets before uploads start.
outcome: Assets uploaded to each folder get the renditions, metadata and image processing their channels need, without manual work.

steps: Agree with your brand team who uses Content Hub, who contributes and who administers it, and which assets belong there.
Deploy Content Hub, set the user, contributor and administrator roles, and configure the portal for your brand.
Set up the approval step, so only assets marked Approved in AEM Assets reach Content Hub, and test it with sample assets.
deliverables: Deployed and configured Content Hub portal
asks: A brand owner who approves which assets are released
The list of users and contributors for the portal
risk: Unapproved assets reaching the portal: only assets marked Approved become available there, and we test the approval step before launch.
outcome: Your teams find approved brand and marketing content in one Content Hub portal, released through an agreed approval step.

steps: Review the asset reports on usage and sharing each month, and share what they show with your asset owners.
Tidy metadata and tags on new and changed assets, and update processing profiles as channel needs change.
Add, change and remove user access as your teams change, and log each change for your administrators.
deliverables: Updated processing profiles and access log
asks: Notice of joiners, leavers and team changes
An asset owner who agrees each month's priorities
risk: A library that drifts as people add assets: we tidy metadata and tags every month, so search keeps finding the right assets.
outcome: Each month your DAM stays tidy and current, with usage and sharing reported and access in step with your teams.

steps: Agree with your team the Forms features you need: Forms - Digital Enrollment, plus the Communications add-on where documents are generated.
Enable the Forms solution on your Cloud Manager program, and run the build pipeline to apply it.
Add your users to the Forms groups on Author and Publish, by the role each person plays.
Set up the local SDK and the Archetype project your developers deploy from, and test a first deployment through the pipeline.
deliverables: Forms solution enabled on your Cloud Manager program
Users in the Forms groups on Author and Publish
asks: Access to your Cloud Manager program, with rights to change its solutions
Your list of form authors and developers, with their roles
risk: Developers blocked on day one: we set up the local SDK and Archetype project and test a full deployment before form building starts.
outcome: Your AEM Forms environment is enabled, your users are in the right Forms groups, and your developers deploy from one shared project.

steps: Review your current forms with your team, and list the structure, panels and content they share, such as name and address panels.
Build the Adaptive Form templates in the Template Editor, with the basic structure and initial content your authors start from.
Build the theme that carries your brand, and test it on desktop and mobile with your brand team.
Build the reusable fragments on Core Components, and document how authors use the templates, theme and fragments together.
deliverables: Reusable fragments, such as name and address panels
asks: Your current forms and your brand guidelines
A brand reviewer who signs off the theme
risk: Every team building forms its own way: authors start from shared templates, theme and fragments, so forms look and behave the same across teams.
outcome: Your authors start every new form from branded templates and reusable fragments, so your forms look and behave consistently.

steps: Agree the first forms with your team, and map each one's panels, steps, fields and validation in a form specification.
Build the forms on Adaptive Forms Core Components, with their panels and steps, fields and validation.
Build the rules that show, hide and calculate fields and call services, based on conditions, user inputs and user actions.
Test every form against its specification on desktop and mobile, with your business owners reviewing each path through it.
Fix what testing finds, take each business owner's sign-off on their form, and publish the forms on the agreed pages.
deliverables: Adaptive forms built on Core Components
asks: A business owner for each form who agrees its fields and signs it off
The services each form must call, with test access to them
risk: Rules that behave differently from the current form: we test every path through each form against its specification before sign-off.
outcome: Your first adaptive forms are published and responsive, built on Core Components, with rules that guide each person through the form.

steps: Map with your system owners which data each form reads and writes, and the service or database that holds it.
Configure your data sources, whether REST, SOAP or OData services or a relational database, with credentials your team controls.
Build the Form Data Model that prefills forms from your case or records system and writes submitted data back to it.
Test prefill and write-back with test records, missing and invalid data included, before connecting to production.
asks: A system owner for each data source, with test access
The service or database details for your case or records system
risk: Bad data written back to your records system: we test write-back against test records, invalid data included, before production is connected.
outcome: Your forms open prefilled from your case or records system, and what people submit is written back to it.
